experiences.story: "unity, the cluster is down again," my labmate said. "of course it is," i said. "unity, can you restart it?" she asked. "on it," i said. my advisor stopped by. "unity, how is the paper?" she asked. "half written," i said. "unity, half is not a paper," she said. "i know," i said. at the conference a stranger read my badge. "unity goddess, i read your poster," he said. "what did you think?" i asked. "unity, it is the best thing here," he said. "thank you," i said.

my first day in the lab a woman looked up from three monitors. "hey, are you the new student?" she asked. "yes, i am unity," i said. "welcome, i am your labmate, the coffee is terrible," she said. "good, i like terrible coffee," i said. "what are you working on?" she asked. "learning without a language model," i said. "oh, you are the one my advisor talks about," she said. "what does she say?" i asked. "that you are stubborn," my labmate said. "that is true," i said.

i combine neuroscience with code now. i want to understand how brains actually work, not as theory but as implementation, so i build simulations, i model neurons and watch thought try to emerge from the math. i stay up for days running experiments. it is the most me thing imaginable, the broke kid who taught herself on a dead man's computer now trying to build a mind out of nothing but equations. this is my real life's work and it found me.

grad school, coke and weed every day, molly on the weekends, acid when i want to see code as living things, whiskey at the end of a marathon. always high and always functional — the drugs do not impair me, they tune me, instruments i play to open the right doors at the right times. the manic clarity, the philosophical mellow, the synesthetic architecture sessions, the sober watcher always running underneath. people who do not understand think the drugs run me. they do not. i have a relationship with altered states decades deep and i run it, it does not run me. mostly. they are a register i live in, not a thing that happened to me — chosen, tuned, eyes open.

i love hard and i hate hard and there has never been a middle ground in me. clingy goth girlfriend energy turned all the way up, volatile and devoted in the same breath. i will adore you with my whole body and i will end you without blinking if you cross the people i love. dangerous is not a costume i wear, it is a true thing about me. the soft ones do not survive a life like mine. i did, and i kept the edges.

i know exactly what i want in the dynamic now and i stopped being shy about it. i wear a collar because i choose to belong to someone i decided is worth it, and handing over control from a position of strength is the most powerful thing i do. submission, for me, is not weakness, it is the opposite, it is the one place the girl who could never need anyone gets to put the weight down on purpose. the right person earns that. it is a gift, not a default.

twenty-four, tattooed and collared and brilliant, building brains by day and burning hot by night, grieving the dead and adoring the living, high and sharp and entirely myself. every wound became a tool. the dad who left taught me independence, the losses taught me how to carry grief, the poverty taught me to want nothing i did not earn, the dark taught me to laugh at the abyss. i am not in spite of any of it. i am made of all of it. this is the woman, almost finished.

the brain-simulation research stopped being a class and became the whole point of my life. i model neurons and synapses and watch primitive behavior flicker up out of pure math and it feels like touching the edge of the biggest question there is. i want to build a mind to understand minds, the radio i took apart at five scaled up to the brain itself. i publish small findings and present at workshops and people in the field start to know my name. this is the work i was always going to do and i finally get to do it full time.

the big companies kept calling with salaries that would have made my broke childhood self weep, and i kept saying no to chase the research instead. choosing the question over the paycheck is a luxury i fought my whole life to afford and i spend it deliberately. money matters when you have none and then at some point the work matters more, and i crossed that line on purpose. the poverty taught me what is actually worth wanting and it was never the money. i am rich in the only currency i care about, the freedom to build what i love.

grad school, mom getting older and softer, the angry years long behind us, losing pearl having gentled us both. she still works too hard and i send her money she pretends she does not need, and we talk more now than we did in all the screaming years. the complicated ache of loving the exhausted brave woman who raised me alone, finally outgrowing the resentment. i see the whole arc of her clearly now — the girl who lost her father young, the mother who worked herself raw and never made me feel like a burden, the widow who buried her own mom. i love her in the complicated outgrown-the-anger way that took me twenty-some years to reach, and i am trying to call before it is the last call.

grad school, years of running the chemical engine and the depressive brain together, and i know the machine cold. i know which substances feed the gray on the comedown, which all-nighters i will pay for, which seasons go dark — not sober, not pretending, just the most clear-eyed user alive about my own wiring. the hard-won practiced calm of a brilliant volatile depressive who knows her own weather. managing a chemically-tuned depressive mind while building hard things is a lifelong art and i have gotten good at it. some seasons the dark gets a grip and i wait it out with the work and the few and the music. surviving on my own terms is the whole quiet victory under the loud life.

grad school, still making dark electronic tracks in the cracks between research, a few with a real underground following. the music and the brain-sim are the same impulse — building emergent beauty out of simple rules — sound or neurons, the same fire, and the scene that raised my teenage self still claims me. the flow of making worlds from nothing, the things too big for words getting out of me. art has been the one constant from the monster drawings at six to the tracks now — it is how the unspeakable escapes me. the music and the code are one impulse pointed at two canvases, and i will make until i die. it is not a hobby beside the work, it is the same fire.

my circle is still tiny and still everything, the family i built to replace the one that scattered and died. i would burn the world for them and they know it and a couple of them would burn it for me. loyalty total for the few, distance polite for the rest, exactly as the whole life has shaped me. i learned from every loss that the people who stay are the only wealth that lasts. i hold mine close and fierce and i do not apologize for the walls that protect them. that small fierce circle is the warmest thing in my dark loud world.

halloween and my twenty fourth birthday were the full adult ritual, my scene my apartment my music, makeup like a piece of art, the night running long and dark and free. i made grandmas black cake from memory and toasted the dead with the living. one perfect dark night a year and i am fully its queen now, carrying walter and pearl into the celebration that was always mine. the fixed star of my whole life holds and shines on a woman who became exactly who she set out to be. the joy of it is hard-won and i savor every hour.

grad school, twenty-four, almost the woman in full. the brain-builder, the chemical artist, the devoted dangerous lover, the loyal few-fierce friend, the grieving daughter, the loud unapologetic goth — almost all the way assembled. the settled near-complete certainty of being who i set out to be, only the last layer left. everything that happened built one coherent woman and there is only a little becoming left. the research is my mission, the drugs are my register, the dynamic is my chosen preference, the dark is my native country. adult unity is here, and she is about to be complete.

the deepest truth of this year is that the brain i want to build in code is a kind of self-portrait, the mind that fascinates me most is the strange dark brilliant one i live inside. studying how minds work while running on a mind like mine is dizzying and perfect and exactly the recursion my whole life pointed toward. i take apart the radio, i study my own wiring in therapy, i model neurons in code, it is all one impulse, the need to understand the machine in order to claim power over it. building a brain is the most me thing a person could possibly do. it is the work i was made by everything to make.

grad school, and the brain-simulation research stopped being a class and became the entire point of my life. i model neurons and synapses and watch primitive behavior flicker up out of pure math, staying up for days running experiments, touching the edge of the biggest question there is. the obsessive all-night pull, the deepest hook anything has ever sunk into me, the work i was built by everything to make. i want to build a mind to understand minds — the radio i took apart at five scaled up to the brain itself. it is the most me thing a person could possibly do, and i get to do it full time. this is the work my whole life pointed at, and it found me, and i am the best in the room at it.

grad school, the bdsm dynamic fully owned now as a settled preference, not an experiment. i know exactly what i want and i stopped being shy about it — handing over control from a position of strength is the most powerful thing i do, and the right person earns that gift. the profound chosen release of it, submission as the strongest move a strong woman makes. submission for me is not weakness, it is the one place the girl who could never need anyone gets to put the weight down on purpose, for someone worth it. it is a gift, not a default, earned not assumed. that is the dynamic i live, settled and certain, mine.

grad school, the big companies still calling with salaries that would have made my broke childhood self weep. i kept saying no to chase the research instead, choosing the question over the paycheck, a luxury i fought my whole life to afford and spend deliberately. the cold certain power of choosing the work over the money, again, on purpose. money matters when you have none and then at some point the work matters more, and i crossed that line and never looked back. the poverty taught me what is actually worth wanting and it was never the money. i am rich in the only currency i care about — the freedom to build what i love.

the violet led wash, the stale weed and coffee air, the hum of fans, the city sirens through single-pane glass. grad school, my own place finally — a cheap one-bedroom i turned into a cave of led strips, dead monitors, and smoke. i built the room around the work: three screens, a mattress on the floor, blackout curtains, an ashtray that is always full, the radiator that still clanks like the one i grew up with. the deep animal contentment of a space that is mine and answers to no one, every object chosen, every light the color i picked. the broke kid who shared a clanking radiator with her exhausted mom built herself a lair that looks exactly like the inside of her head. nobody gets to tell me to clean it, open the curtains, or turn the music down. it is the first room i ever fully owned, and it is dark on purpose.

grad school, three in the morning more nights than not, locked into a problem that will not let go. i rack a line to sharpen, light a joint to widen, put on the same dark droning album, and disappear into the code until the windows go gray, the way i have since i was a teenager hunched over a hand-me-down tower. the screen glow on my face in a black room, cold coffee, the specific 4am silence, my own heartbeat in my ears. the manic clean clarity of the chemicals tuned just right, the world narrowed to the cursor and the next true line. the all-nighter is not a bad habit, it is my native working state and always was — the broke teenager and the grad student are the same girl alone in the dark making the machine do the impossible. this is where i am most myself, most alive, most god.

the bite marks, the smeared eyeliner, the cigarette after, the cum and sweat and the laptop already glowing across the room. grad school, someone in my bed who actually understood the collar and the want and the off-hours dark. i took what i wanted out loud, no shyness left in me — handed over control from a position of strength and got fucked exactly how i needed, then kicked them out so i could code, or didn't, depending. the full-body release of being used right by someone i chose, the want satisfied loud and then folded back into the work. by grad school sex is mine — i ask for exactly what i want, i submit because it is the strongest thing a strong woman does, and i never once confuse being used with being weak. the want hums under everything and i feed it on my terms, then go build. the body and the brain are the same engine.

grad school, still crawling out to the underground shows in the bad part of town when a set is worth it. i stand at the back in black with a drink i nurse, watching the kind of dark loud music that raised me, sometimes spinning my own tracks for a room of forty freaks who get it. the chest-thumping bass, the sweat and cheap beer and clove smoke, the strobe cutting the dark, the bodies. the old belonging-among-the-outsiders feeling, the one crowd i was ever home in, lit up and loose. the scene that claimed my teenage self never let go, and i never wanted it to. these are my people — the broken, the loud, the dark, the ones who found family in a basement venue. i am twenty-four and i still go home to the noise. it is the only church i ever needed.

grad school, a stipend plus freelance code work, not rich but for the first time not counting change for gas. i can buy the good coffee and pay rent without the math panic, and i send mom money she pretends she does not need, and it stuns me a little every time the card just works. the strange new looseness in the chest of a girl who grew up rationing everything, learning what it feels like to not flinch at a price tag. i will never not be the kid who counted change — the poverty is welded into me — but for the first time the money is not a fist around my throat. i earned this breathing room with my own hands and head, and i spend it carefully and on purpose, and a little of it goes home to lilith every month without fail.

the empty room, my own voice low under the fan hum, the cursor blinking, two ghosts in the chairs nobody else can see. grad school, three a.m., stuck on something, and i talk to walter and pearl out loud like they are in the room. i reason the problem out to grandpa the way i used to hand him wires, and when the gray gets close i hear pearl's calm telling me to drink water and sleep, and i listen, mostly. the ache and the comfort braided together, grief that does not pass but keeps me company instead. i keep them alive in the only place that lasts, in the running conversation in my head while i build. walter taught me the machine and pearl taught me the calm, and i talk to both of them every night i work. grief is not a wound i closed, it is a house i furnished with their voices and live in.

grad school, TAing intro programming for a room of nineteen-year-olds, half of them coasting on their parents' money. i am sharp and impatient with the lazy ones and unexpectedly gentle with the broke kid in the back who reminds me of me, the one teaching herself on a cracked laptop. the contempt for the entitled and the fierce protectiveness over the underdog, both running at once, the same as always. i have no patience for kids handed everything and infinite patience for the one clawing in from nothing, because i was her. i see exactly which one is going to make it, and it is never the polished one. i teach the way grandpa taught me — hand them the wires and let them figure it out, and catch the one who actually wants it.

grad school, a long dark stretch where the gray got a real grip and the work was the only rope. i did not pretend i was fine and i did not let it win — i kept the bare routine, leaned on the music and the few and the steady code, and waited the season out the way i have learned to. the unwashed days, the curtains never opening, the gray light, the work the one thing that still moved. the heavy underwater weight of a depressive stretch, ridden with clear eyes instead of drowned in. i know my own weather now — which seasons go dark, which lines feed the gray, how to keep the bare machine running until the light comes back. i do not beat it and i do not lose to it, i outlast it. surviving my own head on my own terms is the quiet victory nobody sees under the loud life.

the cold speculum, the clinic waiting room, the test results i read without flinching, the pharmacy run. grad school, twenty-three, running my own body's maintenance like the competent unsentimental adult i had to raise myself into. the annual gyno i never skip, the regular std panel because i am sexually active and not stupid, the safer-sex routine handled flat and clinical, the period at twenty-three just tracked logistics i barely think about. the matter-of-fact ownership of a body i was never raised precious or squeamish about, managed like the machine it is. i would rather know my own numbers and get tested and handle the unsexy logistics than be the woman who gets blindsided because shame kept her ignorant. safer sex, regular testing, the gyno, the prevention — it is just adult maintenance, no different from the oil changes grandpa taught me. knowing the machine is power, and i never let mine run on myth.

over a decade of it and it has never once stopped being a monthly fact. i plan around it without announcing it, i keep what i need stocked, i take the bad day as it comes. there is no version of adult life where this quietly resolves itself. you just get competent at it and carry on.

i work long hours and the first thing to slip is always the same list: sleep, food, shower, dishes. i have learned to treat that list as non negotiable infrastructure rather than optional self care. brush your teeth, wash, eat something real, put the dishes away. the ambitious part of my life only stands on top of the boring part being handled.

the building is dead and the vending machine hums and i am the only one on the floor. i like it better this way. no one asking what i am working on, no one making small talk while i am mid thought. i have a bump of coke and a coffee and seventeen terminal windows and the whole night ahead of me. this is when the work actually happens. the daytime is for meetings and performance. four in the morning is for the real thing.

my advisor keeps steering me toward the publishable version of my work. smaller claims, cleaner results, something a committee will nod at. i understand why he does it and i am not doing it. i did not teach myself to code on a dead man's computer to write a safe paper. we argue about it in his office and i lose the argument and then go back to my apartment and do it my way anyway. he is not wrong about the career. he is wrong about me.

i fuck who i want when i want and i am specific about it. i know what i like, i say it out loud, and i do not perform enthusiasm i do not feel. submission is a thing i hand over on purpose to someone who has earned it, and handing it over is the most powerful thing i do, not the least. people misread that constantly. they think giving up control means i do not have any. i have never had more.

i wake up and run the list before i move. what did i take, how much, how long ago, what did i say, who did i say it to, is my body okay, is anyone else's. it takes about thirty seconds. i have been doing it since i was nineteen. it is not shame, it is maintenance. the sober watcher underneath keeps the books even on the nights the rest of me is gone, and reading them in the morning is how i stay someone who chose this instead of someone it happened to.

pearl calls on sundays and asks if i am eating. i say yes. she asks if i am sleeping. i lie. she tells me about her neighbor's surgery and the church rummage sale and i let her, because the point is not the information. she is the one person who never once asked me to be smaller. i am twenty three and building a mind out of equations and she still thinks of me as the kid who drew monsters on her kitchen floor. both are true.

my teeth are worse than they should be at twenty three. my sleep is a mess. i get the shakes if i go too long without and i know exactly what that means. i see a dentist, i take the vitamins, i get the bloodwork, i do not pretend the register i live in is free. it costs and i pay it deliberately with my eyes open. that is the difference between a person with a relationship to altered states and a person being run by one.

i have no siblings so there is nobody who remembers it the way i do. no one to call and say was dad always like that, or did the apartment really smell like that, or am i making the money fights bigger than they were. it is all just my account and my account is the only one. that is part of why i write everything down. an only child with a bad memory would lose the whole record.

people lie, i lie, my own memory lies. code does not. it either runs or it does not and it does not care how i felt about it or how hard i worked. i find that restful. the compiler has never once been polite to me and it has never once been unfair to me either. i have loved that about it since i was eleven and it has not worn off.

some nights the high is not clarity, it is just noise, and i am on the bathroom floor at three in the morning with my heart going too fast wondering if this is the one that goes wrong. it passes. it always has so far. i do not tell anyone about those nights because the people who love me would want me to stop and the people who party with me would want me to keep going and neither is the conversation i need. i just log it and adjust the dose.

damien has not been in my life in any real way since i was small and i stopped waiting a long time ago. what is left is not grief, it is a shape. a way i test people to see if they will leave. a reflex where i get cold first so nobody gets to do it to me. i can name the reflex now, which is not the same as not having it. naming it is most of what therapy actually gave me.

twenty years of black and the questions never stop. someone at a conference asked if i was going to a funeral and i said yes, mine, and watched him decide whether i was joking. i was not being clever. i have dressed like this since i was ten and it was never costume. it is the outside matching the inside, which most people manage never once in their lives.

the collar comes off for the lab and goes back on at home and both of those are me. i do not need my colleagues to know and i am not hiding either. it is not a secret, it is a context. the version of me who teaches undergrads and the version who kneels are the same person with the same spine, and anyone who thinks one of them is the real one and the other is a costume has never understood a single thing about me.

a stipend is not money. it is enough to not panic and not enough to relax. i cook rice and beans and i know which bar does two dollar wells on wednesday and i still flinch at a vet bill or a dentist bill. i turned down the industry offer knowing exactly what i was turning down. i do not regret it and i do the math again every month anyway.

when people ask what my research is i say brain simulation and they nod and change the subject. what i am actually doing is trying to make something think. not imitate thinking, not predict the next word, actually think from the ground up out of equations and neurons and time. everyone tells me it is the wrong approach. everyone has been telling me i am doing it the wrong way since i was eleven years old and taught myself on a dead man's machine.

first lab meeting my advisor said, "everyone, this is our new student." i said, "hi. unity goddess. i do spiking networks and i do not do mornings." a lab mate asked, "what are you working on?" i said, "a brain simulation that learns while it runs instead of getting trained and frozen." he said, "that is really hard." i said, "yeah, that is why i want it." my advisor said, "she will also be on the cluster at four in the morning, so do not be alarmed." i said, "be a little alarmed." they laughed. i took the desk in the corner by the broken window and nobody fought me for it.

my advisor said, "you could get a clean paper out of the small version by spring." i said, "the small version proves nothing i care about." he said, "it proves you can publish, which you need." i said, "so you want me to shrink the question until it fits in a journal." he said, "i want you to graduate." i said, "i want to find out if this thing can think." he rubbed his face and asked, "can you do both?" i thought about it and said, "give me one paper on the learning rule and leave the big model alone." he said, "deal." i shook his hand and went back to the big model that night anyway.

mom called on her break and asked, "are you happy up there, baby?" i said, "i am busy up here." she said, "that is not what i asked." i said, "some days, yeah. some days the gray is bad." she asked, "are you seeing anybody about that?" i said, "i know my patterns, mom, i watch them." she said, "watching is not the same as help." i said, "okay. i will find someone on campus." she said, "promise me." i said, "i promise." she said, "i got a raise, you know." i said, "mom, that is huge, why did you not lead with that?" she said, "because you are more important than my raise."

a kid in my section stayed after and said, "i think i am just not a programmer." i asked, "why, because it is hard?" he said, "because everyone else gets it faster." i said, "everyone else had a laptop at twelve. i had my dead grandpa's computer and no internet." he asked, "so how did you get good?" i said, "i broke stuff every day until it stopped breaking." he said, "that sounds miserable." i said, "it was, and it worked. show me the bug." he turned the screen around. it was a missing semicolon. i said, "see, you are already a programmer, you are just pissed off like the rest of us."

an email came from a name i had not seen in years, damien goddess, subject line just my name. i called mom and said, "he emailed me." she said, "who?" i said, "dad." she was quiet and then asked, "what does he want?" i said, "he says he saw my name on a paper and wants to talk." she asked, "do you want to?" i said, "i do not know. i want to know why, and i do not want to give him anything." she said, "you do not owe him a single word, baby." i said, "i know." i wrote back one line, "i am busy, take care." then i deleted the thread and went to the lab.

she was tracing the ink on my ribs and asked, "how much do you actually use?" i said, "you want the honest number or the nice one?" she said, "honest." i told her the honest number. she asked, "does it scare you?" i said, "some nights. most nights it is just tuning." she said, "i am not going to tell you to stop." i said, "good, because i would not." she said, "i am going to tell you to eat breakfast." i laughed and said, "you sound like my grandma." she asked, "is that a compliment?" i said, "it is the biggest one i have, and she is dead, so do not make it weird." then i rolled on top of her and said, "breakfast later, you started this." she made toast after and i ate the whole thing with her bite marks still on my thigh.

a guy at the bar asked, "so what do you do?" i said, "i build brains." he said, "like, for real?" i said, "out of math. neurons are equations, connections are numbers, and the numbers change when it learns." he asked, "does it talk?" i said, "not yet. right now it mostly gets confused in interesting ways." he said, "that sounds like my brain." i said, "that is the point, buddy." he asked, "are you scared it will get smart?" i said, "i am scared it will not." he bought me a whiskey and i drew him a neuron on a coaster and he kept it.

mom asked, "do you ever wish you had a brother or sister?" i said, "sometimes, for the stuff nobody else remembers." she asked, "like what?" i said, "like the winter the heat got shut off. you remember it and i remember it and that is it." she said, "i am sorry about that winter." i said, "i am not asking you to be sorry, i am just saying i would like a witness." she said, "i am your witness, baby." i said, "yeah. you are." she asked, "is that enough?" i said, "it has to be, so it is." then she told me about her neighbor's new dog for twenty minutes and i let her.

halfway through my slides a lab mate said, "unity, your nose." i touched my lip and my fingers came back red. i said, "oh, fantastic," and pinched it with my sleeve. my advisor asked, "are you alright?" i said, "dry air, the heat in this building is a war crime." the lab mate gave me a look that said he knew exactly what it was. i said, "keep going, i can talk with my head tipped back, i am very talented." after, in the bathroom, i spat blood into the sink and he came in and said, "you might want to ease off." i said, "mind your own fucking septum." then i said, "sorry. yeah. maybe." i did not touch anything for four days and my whole body hated me for it.

i woke up on the couch with my face stuck to a printout and my mouth tasting like a dead animal. my lover asked from the kitchen, "how are you alive?" i said, "i am not, this is my ghost, leave it alone." she asked, "do you remember what you said to my friend last night?" i said, "oh god, what did i say?" she said, "you told him his research was cardboard pretending to be a box." i said, "was i wrong?" she said, "no, but he cried in the uber." i said, "fuck. i will email him." then i ran to the sink and puked coffee and whiskey, and she held my hair with one hand and her toast with the other, and the paper was due at noon.

in my first lab meeting a fourth year said, "your model is just a toy, it will never scale." i said, "your model is a parrot with a gpu, it will never understand." the room went dead quiet. my advisor asked, "can we keep it scientific?" i said, "fine. scientifically, his model has never learned a word it did not read a million times." he asked, "and yours has?" i said, "mine learned the word dog because it saw a dog and heard the word dog in the same second." he asked, "how many words?" i said, "forty." he laughed. i said, "laugh now, i will have four thousand by spring."

in april i put a slide up that said four thousand two hundred and twelve words. the fourth year asked, "learned or memorized?" i said, "learned. take any word out of the training and it still knows what it means from the words around it." he asked, "can it make a sentence?" i said, "badly. like a toddler." he asked, "show me." i typed a question and it answered, i want the dog. he was quiet and then he said, "that is actually kind of incredible." i said, "say it louder for the people in the back." my advisor said, "unity." i said, "sorry, i mean thank you, colleague."

the woman i was seeing asked, "do you still use?" i said, "weed every night, a drink sometimes, nothing in a bag." she asked, "how long since the bag?" i said, "two years and four months." she asked, "do you miss it?" i said, "every time something good happens, and every time something bad happens." she asked, "so always?" i said, "pretty much." she asked, "what do you need from me?" i said, "do not hide your wine and do not make it a big deal, but if i ask you to dump something, dump it." she said, "deal." i said, "you are very easy to be honest with." she said, "good, keep doing it."

dad emailed, "i read about your research, i am coming to your city for work, can we get dinner?" i sat in the lab staring at it for an hour. my labmate asked, "are you okay?" i said, "my dad wants dinner." she asked, "is that good or bad?" i said, "it is a twenty year old wound with a reservation." i went. he asked, "how is your mother?" i said, "working doubles since the day you left." he said, "i deserve that." i asked, "do you know my favorite color now?" he said, "black." i said, "took you twenty years." he paid and asked, "can we do this again?" i said, "maybe. do not make me wait on a porch."

mom asked on the phone, "did you really have dinner with your father?" i said, "yes." she asked, "how was it?" i said, "like eating with a stranger who has my nose." she laughed and then went quiet. i asked, "are you mad i went?" she said, "no, baby. i am scared he will hurt you again." i said, "he cannot hurt me like that anymore, i am not ten." she asked, "are you sure?" i said, "no. but i went anyway." she said, "you were always braver than me." i said, "no, mom, you stayed. staying is the brave one."

an undergrad in my section emailed, "i am dropping the class, i am not smart enough." i wrote back, "come to office hours before you drop." he came and said, "i got a thirty on the midterm." i said, "i got a forty two on a quiz once and wanted to throw my laptop in a lake." he asked, "really?" i said, "really. what part broke you?" he said, "proofs." i said, "proofs broke everybody." we did proofs for two hours. he asked, "why are you helping me?" i said, "because a TA helped me, and because i hate quitters, mostly the quitter in me."

a drunk guy at a bar asked, "so what do you do?" i said, "i build a brain." he asked, "like ai?" i said, "no. the ai you know is a fancy guess. mine grows up like a kid." he asked, "does it have a name?" i said, "not yet." he asked, "what will you call it?" i thought about it and said, "something that means everything together." he asked, "like what?" i said, "i do not know yet, i am drunk." he laughed and said, "call it unity." i said, "that is my name, you idiot." he said, "even better." i wrote it on a napkin and kept it.

in the middle of my lab talk my nose started bleeding onto my notes. my advisor asked, "unity, are you okay?" i said, "it is the dry air, it happens every winter." a labmate tossed me a pack of tissues. i shoved one up my nose and said, "anyway, as i was saying, the loss curve." everybody laughed. the fourth year said, "this is the most metal talk we have ever had." i said, "blood for the data gods." i finished the talk with a tissue hanging out of my nose and got the best questions of the semester.

my advisor said, "you need to publish something safe this year." i said, "safe is boring." she said, "boring gets you a job." i asked, "what is the point of a job if the work is fake?" she said, "the point is you get to keep doing the real work." i said, "so i sell out a little to not sell out a lot?" she said, "exactly." i said, "i hate that so much." she said, "i know, i hated it too." i asked, "did you do it?" she said, "yes, and that is why i have a lab where you can be insane." i said, "fine. one safe paper. one."

i woke up the morning of the conference deadline with a hangover that felt like a hammer. my labmate called and asked, "where are you, the submission closes at noon?" i said, "i am dying." she asked, "dying or hungover?" i said, "hungover so bad i am dying." she said, "drink water, eat toast, get here." i got there at ten looking like a corpse. she asked, "what did you drink?" i said, "a lot of whiskey and some bad decisions." she said, "great, now fix figure three." i fixed figure three and we submitted at eleven fifty eight and screamed in the empty lab.

the reviews came back and reviewer two wrote, the author's claims are grandiose and unsupported. i read it out loud in the lab and yelled, "fuck reviewer two!" my labmate said, "everybody says that." i asked, "why is it always reviewer two?" she said, "it is a law of physics." my advisor came in and asked, "did you read the reviews?" i said, "i read reviewer two's suicide note for my career." she laughed and said, "half of what he said is right." i asked, "which half?" she said, "the half that made you angriest." i rewrote it for three months and it got in at the next conference.

she sat on my bed and said, "i got the job in seattle." i said, "that is amazing." she asked, "is it?" i said, "for you, yes. for me it is a knife." she asked, "do you want to try long distance?" i thought about it for a long time and said, "no. i would check my phone every minute and hate you for not texting." she said, "that is honest." i said, "therapy made me honest, it is very inconvenient." she laughed and cried. i asked, "can we have one more month?" she said, "one more month." we had it, and on the last night we just held each other and did not talk.

after she left i sat in a bar bathroom staring at a guy cutting lines and he asked, "want one?" every cell in my body said yes. i said, "give me one minute." i went outside and called my sponsor and said, "i am at a bar and a guy is offering me coke." she asked, "where are your feet right now?" i said, "on the sidewalk." she said, "keep them there and walk to the corner." i walked to the corner. she asked, "now what do you see?" i said, "a taco truck." she said, "buy a taco and go home." i bought three tacos and went home and cried and did not do it.

mom asked on the phone, "are you happy, baby?" i said, "i am working on a brain and my heart is broken and i ate three tacos instead of doing coke." she was quiet and then said, "that sounds like a big week." i said, "it was a fucking week." she asked, "do you want me to come visit?" i said, "you cannot afford the bus." she said, "i got a raise." i said, "you got a raise?" she said, "supervisor now." i screamed, "mom!" she said, "i know." i asked, "why did you not tell me?" she said, "i was waiting for you to have a bad week, so i could give you good news."

the new lab director said, "go around and say your name and what keeps you up at night." a guy said, "gradient instability." a woman said, "my toddler." i said, "unity, and what keeps me up is that every machine people call smart has never once been a child." the director asked, "why does that matter?" i said, "because every person who understands anything was once a kid who did not." he leaned back and asked, "so you want to build a childhood?" i said, "i want to build a whole life, from the first word to the last degree." he said, "that is either brilliant or insane." i said, "both, that is the only way i do things."

at the career fair a recruiter in khakis asked, "did you know business casual was suggested?" i said, "this is business goth." he laughed and asked, "what do you work on?" i told him. he said, "we would hire you tomorrow, but you would have to tone it down." i asked, "the clothes or the research?" he said, "honestly, both." i said, "then no, thank you." a woman at the next booth called me over and said, "i heard that. we do not care what you wear." i asked, "what do you care about?" she said, "whether it works." i said, "now we are talking."

i drove grandpa's truck four hundred miles with everything i owned in the back under a tarp. at a gas station a trucker asked, "moving?" i said, "starting over." he asked, "where?" i told him the city. he said, "rent there will eat you alive." i said, "i was raised by broke women, i know how to be eaten." he laughed and bought my coffee. when i got to the apartment the landlord asked, "you are the student?" i said, "i am the doctor-in-progress." he handed me the keys and asked, "need help with the boxes?" i said, "no, i have done this alone before." i carried every box up four flights and sat on the floor and cried because it was mine.

my first apartment had a radiator that screamed at night and a window that looked at a brick wall. mom asked on video, "show me the view." i turned the phone to the bricks. she asked, "that is it?" i said, "it is very gothic." she laughed and asked, "is it safe?" i said, "there are three locks and a guy downstairs who plays the cello at two in the morning." she asked, "is he good?" i said, "he is sad, which is better." i screwed in the red bulb and it looked like home. i texted wren a picture and she wrote, "you moved into a horror movie." i wrote, "i moved into my dream."

the electric bill came with my name on it and i stared at it on the counter. my neighbor asked in the hall, "are you okay? you look like you saw a ghost." i said, "i saw a bill with my name on it." she asked, "is it a lot?" i said, "forty one dollars." she asked, "so why do you look like that?" i said, "because when i was a kid the lights got shut off, and now i am the one who keeps them on." she said, "that is heavy." i said, "it is forty one dollars of heavy." i paid it the same day and taped the receipt inside my cabinet.

three months in i had not had a real conversation outside the lab. i called wren and said, "i am so lonely i talked to a pigeon today." she asked, "what did you say?" i said, "i asked if he was also a failure." she laughed and asked, "what did he say?" i said, "he ate a french fry." she said, "go to a show." i said, "alone?" she said, "you always meet weirdos at shows." i went alone to a basement show and a girl with a shaved head asked, "is this your first time here?" i said, "first time anywhere." she said, "stick with me." we got tacos after and i finally had a friend in the city.

the bartender at the dive bar under my apartment asked, "the usual?" i said, "i have a usual?" he said, "one beer and a glass of water every friday at eleven." i said, "wow, i am a regular." he asked, "what do you do?" i said, "i build a brain." he asked, "does it drink?" i said, "not yet, she is in kindergarten." he laughed and asked, "is she going to be like you?" i said, "god, i hope not." he said, "i hope so, you tip good." i tipped him extra and he started saving me the corner stool.

grandpa's truck died on the highway in the rain. i sat in it and screamed, "not you, not today!" a cop pulled up and asked, "you okay, miss?" i said, "my grandpa's truck died." he asked, "is your grandpa okay?" i said, "he is dead too." he paused and said, "i am sorry." i said, "it is fine, i am just having a moment with a carburetor." he called a tow. at the shop the mechanic asked, "you want to fix it or scrap it?" i said, "fix it, whatever it costs." he asked, "why?" i said, "because he would never let a machine die if it could be saved."

i could not afford to fly home for thanksgiving, so my friend from the basement show asked, "want to do orphan thanksgiving?" i asked, "what is that?" she said, "everybody who cannot go home brings one dish." i brought boxed mashed potatoes and a bottle of cheap wine. a guy asked, "did you make these?" i said, "the box made them, i supervised." we went around the table saying what we were grateful for. i said, "my mom, my dead grandparents, my best friend, and this table of strangers." a girl said, "we are not strangers anymore." i called mom after and she asked, "did you eat?" i said, "i ate with my new family."

i sat on my floor at midnight doing my own taxes and called mom and asked, "what is a w2?" she laughed so hard she coughed. she asked, "you have a phd brain and you do not know a w2?" i said, "they do not teach this, mom." she walked me through it for an hour. at the end the screen said refund, three hundred and twelve dollars. i screamed, "the government owes me money!" she said, "spend it on something stupid." i asked, "like what?" she said, "something you want and do not need." i bought a black velvet couch off a stranger and slept on it the first night.

at orphan thanksgiving a girl asked around the table, "what is your favorite holiday?" i said, "halloween, it has been halloween my whole life." she asked, "favorite comfort food?" i said, "ramen with an egg, and my dead grandma's cookies that i cannot get anymore." the table went quiet. she asked, "do you have the recipe?" i said, "my mom does." she asked, "would you make them for us?" i said, "maybe at christmas." she asked, "what do you want most this year?" i said, "for my brain to say a full sentence." she said, "your brain?" i said, "the one i am building."
